demand_source.title: Talk mode
demand_source.anchor: Native Talk is a continuous loop
demand_source.supports: OpenClaw documents Talk in its phone apps as a supported continuous speech conversation: it listens, sends the transcript to the agent and speaks the reply.

edits.how: The App Store OpenClaw app on Tony's iPhone, the same install and pairing as the iPhone app entry (OCL-01), reaching the gateway over the tailnet (the app connects over LAN or tailnet; this gateway is Tailscale Serve only). Before pairing: the phone command ceiling is in place (device commands denied first; see the iPhone app entry OCL-01 and the gateway-wide node deny list MAC-04); `talk.agentId` is set explicitly and names a memory-less agent, because it is one value for the whole gateway and receives every Talk session that arrives without an agent-prefixed key; `tts.modelOverrides.allowProvider` stays off (its default) so a reply directive cannot move speech to a cloud provider; and the operator's inspect script gains a read-only listing of paired devices and their scopes. Tony generates the pairing code with `openclaw qr --limited` instead of the default admin handoff. `--voice-node` is not for this phone: it drops the write scope, so typed chat (`chat.send`) and the Listen action (`tts.speak`) stop working, and whether Talk still runs is untested. Native Talk is a loop: Apple Speech recognition on the phone, Gateway chat on the agent picked in the app (tony-main), then `talk.speak` playback. `talk.speak` reads the Talk block, not the `tts` block: set `talk.provider` plus `talk.providers.<id>` to a speech provider (the local speech engine set up for voice over iMessage, F003, can be named there); with no Talk provider the gateway call fails and the docs mention an iPhone system-voice fallback. Other keys: `talk.speechLocale`, `talk.silenceTimeoutMs`, `talk.interruptOnSpeech`. Entry points: the inline Talk control, the `Start Live Voice` App Shortcut, the Siri phrase, or the Action Button. Later option, realtime voice: a `talk.realtime` block with `provider` openai, a realtime model from the installed docs, `transport` webrtc and `brain` agent-consult, so every tool call still goes through gateway policy on the agent. The iPhone path is client-owned WebRTC and needs an OpenAI Platform API key under `talk.realtime.providers.openai`, supplied as a SecretRef and separate from the per-person chat keys. Once that block is set, OpenAI realtime configs run as WebRTC on the iPhone and only non-realtime configs use the native loop. The host asks for a fresh spoken yes before a high-impact action started by voice.
depends_on: the OpenClaw iPhone app paired on Tony's phone with device commands denied first (OCL-01, and the node deny list in MAC-04)
a Talk speech provider under `talk.provider` (the local speech engine from F003), or accept the iPhone system-voice fallback

Dictating an iMessage to Happy with the keyboard microphone or Siri already works today with no setup, and voice over iMessage (F003, wave A) gives both parents voice memos in and spoken replies out with speech kept on the Mac mini. Talk adds only the continuous hands-free loop and being able to interrupt, for Tony alone; it is not a new capability.

Everything about the pairing applies here unchanged and is spelled out in the iPhone app entry (OCL-01): the app is a gateway client first, every pairing profile includes operator.read (session lists, chat history, logs and read-only browsing of every agent's workspace), `--limited` removes only operator.admin and leaves write, approvals and Talk secrets, the phone registers as a node, App Store builds use a vendor-hosted push relay, and a lost phone has to be revoked on the gateway. On a second adult's phone the other adult's agent memory would be readable.
`--voice-node` does not rescue the native loop: the chat turn is chat.send, which the docs class as write-scoped, and that profile holds only read and talk.

Talk playback uses the Talk speech provider, not the general tts block. The docs name elevenlabs (cloud), mlx and system for Talk, and the mlx helper ships with the Mac app, which is not installed here; expect the iPhone's own system voice.

`openclaw qr` only advertises a Tailscale URL when OpenClaw itself owns the Serve route (`gateway.tailscale.mode`). The config repo sets it to serve on a loopback bind, so this looks met; confirm on the live gateway. mDNS discovery is off there, so pairing is by QR or setup code.

A phone paired without operator.admin cannot open the app's Settings pages, where this device's Talk, Voice Wake, background-listening and speakerphone switches live. Plan on the inline Talk control in Chat and the Start Live Voice shortcut.

Realtime option: raw audio, not just text, goes to OpenAI for the whole call (with WebRTC the media runs directly between the phone and the provider), under 30 days of abuse-monitoring retention unless the organisation has Zero Data Retention; the M1 store-off setting covers chat calls only. edits.how: Step 1, read-only (F081): a command payload with no model runs openhue and sonos status on the Gateway host at 22:30 and prints `NO_REPLY` when everything is off; nothing is actuated. Step 2, switching: a sandboxed, stateless home agent reached by `sessions_spawn` holds two in-house plugins. Hue (F076) wraps the openhue CLI on the host, with the bridge key in ~/.openhue/config.yaml, a room allowlist and quiet hours in code. Sonos (F077) wraps the sonos CLI: favourites and allowlisted scenes only, a volume cap and a lower night cap in code; it needs the macOS Local Network permission for the gateway's node process, or `--ip` per speaker. Scheduled bedtime scenes are left to the Hue app, and the other bundled device skills stay uninstalled. Later option, Home Assistant as the single route (a separate, large piece of work that replaces the two plugins; the home agent stays): run Home Assistant OS in a VM on the Mac mini (the roadmap already plans this VM for the kids' speaker, VOX-11). Add the Hue, Sonos and LG webOS integrations, then the 'Model Context Protocol Server' integration; turn off 'Expose all LLM APIs' and expose only the wanted entities. In OpenClaw add mcp.servers.<name> with url http://<ha-host>:8123/api/mcp, transport 'streamable-http' written out (when it is omitted OpenClaw uses sse), and the Home Assistant long-lived token in headers.Authorization, supplied through a secret reference and not a config literal (auth 'oauth' with openclaw mcp login is the documented alternative). This Gateway uses tools.profile 'minimal', which hides MCP tools, so grant them only to the stateless home agent by listing the <server>__<tool> names in that agent's alsoAllow and in its sandbox tool allow list (tools.sandbox.tools.alsoAllow); no other agent then sees the server. Write toolFilter.include after a live probe (openclaw mcp doctor <name> --probe), since it selects tools by name. The registry before_tool_call hook stays as the second, fail-closed gate and enforces quiet hours. Announcements: Home Assistant's Sonos integration plays speech with its `announce` option as an overlay, lowering the music and restoring the volume afterwards; it needs TCP port 1443 on each speaker to be reachable from the Home Assistant host. Because the MCP server offers intents and exposed scripts only, a parent writes one Home Assistant script that wraps the announce call and exposes it, and picks a local speech engine in Home Assistant, since its text-to-speech page also lists cloud engines. The trigger is deterministic: a `before_dispatch` claim on a fixed prefix such as `announce:` from an adult's handle, so no agent that reads web results decides to speak to the house. The code that claims the text then starts the Home Assistant script itself, with no model turn, through Home Assistant's REST API (`/api/services/<domain>/<service>` with the same host-side bearer token); that call path is a design choice and was not tried. The first version offers a short list of fixed phrases; the parent's own words, verbatim, come later, and model-written text never. Text length, volume, quiet hours (G001), a speaker allowlist and a daily cap are enforced in code.

edits.safety: Switching is the riskier part: the home agent can change lights and speakers, so it is stateless, holds no family data, has no web tool and no outbound message tool, is reached only by a bounded hand-off, and its limits live in code. The goodnight check is read-only, runs no model and switches nothing. Locks, garage, alarm and gate are never included. demand_source.title: System prompt: long-running-work guidance
demand_source.supports: OpenClaw's built-in guidance tells an agent to handle future follow-up, such as checking back later and recurring work, with scheduled jobs; together with the vendor's advice to keep a longer aim in a project note with a review date (already on the item) this is the feature's pattern.

caveats: Scheduled runs do not get MEMORY.md injected, so a check-in must read the project note with a tool or carry the state in the job message.
A job created from chat is capped to the tools the creating turn had and cannot be widened later, so a check-in can never do more than the parent's own main agent.
The conversation resets every morning at 04:00 and that also wipes any /goal; the project note is the only continuity between days.
Every check-in is a cloud model turn. Pace in days, not minutes, and cap active projects per person (three is plenty).
No bookings, purchases or invitations sent: the output is options, links and drafts. A static checklist is still easier in a shared Notes or Reminders list; Happy adds the nudging and the research.

Command-owner status is gateway-wide: an owner can ask their agent to list, inspect, update, run or remove any job on the gateway, whoever created it. Once Jordan is an owner, each parent's agent can read and change the other's check-in jobs, so job messages must not carry private detail.

The F041 plan refuses memory writes in a turn tainted by web results, and a turn that received a research result is tainted. Research findings therefore cannot be saved into the project note in that turn: they stay in the chat thread, and the note holds only what the parent states or confirms afterwards.

OpenClaw's own guidance is to deny the scheduling tool by default on any agent that handles untrusted content (docs/gateway/security/tool-permissions.md).

-main with a `pacing` object (`min`, `max`; `--pacing-min` and `--pacing-max` are the CLI spelling), so each run can call `automations(action: "next_check")` and be clamped to those bounds. The job's tool cap holds the note or home-store read tools plus `automations` (inside an automation run that tool is limited to the run's own job) and never `sessions_spawn` or a web tool; announce to the owner; NO_REPLY when nothing is due; the run removes its own job after the end date. Hard prerequisites before `automations` is allowed on

-main: the fail-closed before_tool_call pin must also match `automations`/`cron` add and update and refuse webhook delivery, completion and failure destinations, and any recipient other than the asking parent; and `cron.triggers.enabled: false`, so the tool does not offer script payloads, trigger scripts or stream commands.
